hubs.state: The ley line under Monroe Park ran off-tempo for the fourth time in seven weeks, now detected by unofficial instruments. Dr. Olave's closed meetings continue, and the engineered Awakening program remains secret.
hubs.condition: Consilium fracture widening; Olave's closed meetings have grown more exclusive and a second, smaller meeting now convenes; Ingrid Voss's archival inquiries have reached restricted Special Collections material. Junior faculty and Consilium members are tracking who is no longer invited.

hubs.note: Increased supernatural activity near the warehouse; Petra Holt's principals are now active in the area.
Increased hunter network activity near The Exchange.
rumors: A contract Augustine Pell sealed on Main Street reads differently this week, and his seal is still on it.
Every Main Street board calendar has a 3 a.m. meeting that nobody booked.
One of Ambrose Kettering's sealed lock chambers under Main Street was opened from the inside.
hubs.condition: Night-shift unease at The Exchange has sharpened: a mortal medium has begun waiting through the late shift and leaving offerings at a second Downtown location, and staff continue to log unlogged traffic no known network claims.

Temporal displacement continues to surface through ordinary institutional routines. The East End Family Resource Center's pantry intake keeps logging names and vouchers that don't match current RRHA records, and Sister Catherine Burke's separate ledger for them has grown as she cross-checks the entries against older parish records.
rumors: Tobias Mensah's night bus picked up a rider with a 1987 transfer slip who asked for a building that came down in 2019.
This week's jars of Miss Odessa's honey are labelled with a year that has not happened yet.
J-Rock's newest mural shows the Renaissance return vote, and the count is already painted in.
Someone at the redevelopment field office is asking which families got relocation letters dated before they moved in.
The Midnight Truck's jingle was heard on a block that was cleared last spring.
The chain net on the old court rang all night, and at dawn the blacktop showed the chalk score of a 1974 game.
Emmett Daye has stopped mowing past the grave with a living man's burial date; he says the date moved a week closer.
The newest name on the War Memorial wall matches a man who signed its guest book yesterday.
Headstone letters Gail Brannock recut last month now spell different names.
A younger Night crew has started meeting on Gambles Hill on purpose, just to test Hester Byrd.
Felix Marchbanks is looking for the families behind a box of service medals that came in with no estate attached.
Kelechi Nwosu's tow contract marked a car parked in a Hollywood section that Emmett says was not there last week.
The night crews were paid this week in envelopes printed with the name of a bank that closed in the 1940s.
Dee Ashby's logbook lists a man the river gave back who has not gone into the water yet.
Hollis Grey's newest floodplain map shows streets under the terminal that match an old plat of Warwick.
The terminal's night dispatcher refused to berth a barge on Thursday's tide and will not say why.
Anglers on the Belle Isle rocks lost three hours on Sunday night, and all of them came home with the same fish.
Somebody broke a promise to the river at the Mayo Bridge, and the Lady of the Falls is asking who.
Under the viaduct, a phone stuck on 1958 took a call from a number that was disconnected in 1958.
Someone is buying up motel lots on the strip, and the buyer has never signed Mr. Lacey's register.
The annex's late docket listed three defendants nobody can find in any record.
Tally Monroe's van picked up a woman at the annex curb who gave an address that has been under the viaduct since it was built.
Darnell Hayes is fixing a bike that came in wearing a 1958 license tag, and its rider has not come back for it.
The Lamplighter Holding Center's state audit was moved up a month, and Gideon Marsh has not slept since.
A stenographer in the council chamber swears the minutes now say her morning's motion passed unanimously, and she remembers it failing.
The City Hall parking deck's third level keeps a numbered space that no permit lists, and a car sits there every night until sunrise.
A bill that died in committee last spring appeared on this week's calendar with its original sponsor's name on it, and the sponsor says she never filed it.
Someone has been leaving fresh flowers at the Capitol's gallery door, and the doorkeeper's pillar is always warm in the morning.
A records clerk found a deed in the vault with today's date, signed in handwriting from 1912.
A storefront near Capitol Square is offering free help with city paperwork, and everyone who accepted has since stopped being able to find their own old forms.
